text:
# The Corridor

The kitchen on the fourth floor of Flogsta had a window facing another kitchen in the next building, and in winter, when dark came at half past two, you could watch strangers make pasta like actors in a play nobody had bought tickets for. I spent most of my second year at Uppsala watching them. Later I understood why: I preferred lives I could see all of and didn't have to be in.

Carl was my boyfriend. He studied economics and folded his receipts in half before putting them in his wallet. We met at a nation pub, where he bought me a cider and then, apologizing, asked me to pay him back because he was on a strict budget. I found this endearing. I still do, though for a while that year I worked hard to find it contemptible. He was kind. I want to say that early, before I say everything else.

Lizzy lived two doors down, an exchange student from Leeds who entered rooms as if they had been waiting for her. She wore men's coats from Myrorna and smoked on the balcony at minus fifteen, holding the cigarette in her mitten. On my birthday she baked a cake shaped like the cathedral, and when it collapsed she served it anyway and called it "the Reformation." Everybody laughed. I remember thinking nothing I did would ever make eleven people laugh at once, and that being her friend was the next best thing.

Johan lived across the hall. He was training as a hospital chemist and baked bread late at night, because the oven was free and he couldn't sleep anyway. For most of autumn I knew him only as the smell of rye at one in the morning. Lizzy called him "the Monk."

And then there was Martin.

Martin was a philosophy doctoral student who, in November, started a Thursday reading group on Simone Weil. I went because Lizzy wanted to; she'd seen him at a party and said he had "a face like a disappointed saint." He was thirty-one, wore the same gray sweater every week, and paused before answering questions, eyes on the ceiling, as if the answer were written there in very small print. The first week, I said something about Weil's idea that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity, and he looked at me, paused, and said, "Yes. That's exactly it. Say more."

I want to be precise, because for a long time I described it wrongly. I did not fall in love with Martin. I fell in love with the version of myself who was being asked to say more. At home I had been the quiet, reliable one. With Carl I was the one who agreed that lentils were good. In that seminar room I was someone with thoughts worth waiting for.

By December he was walking me to the bus stop afterward, and we would let one bus go by, sometimes two. When I said I didn't know what I wanted from life, he said, "Good. The people who know are usually lying." I wrote that down when I got home.

I told Lizzy all of it. That was our arrangement: I lived things slowly, then brought them to her, and she held them up to the light. "Oh, he's absolutely gone for you," she would say on the balcony, thrilled. I didn't notice that she had stopped coming to the group.

Carl noticed I had changed. He didn't say anything; he just tried harder. He bought saffron, which must have cost him a week of budgeting, and asked what Simone Weil was about. I explained impatiently. He nodded and said, "That sounds hard. To pay attention like that." I felt a flash of irritation that he had understood, because I had wanted it to belong to Martin and me.

In January, at the bus stop on Dag Hammarskjölds väg, with snow coming sideways, Martin kissed me. Or I kissed him; I honestly don't know. It lasted perhaps four seconds. Then he stepped back and said, "We shouldn't make this into something it isn't." I said, "No, of course not," and rode the bus to the end of the line and back, because I couldn't stand being seen in the corridor.

When I got home past midnight, Johan was in the kitchen, flour to the elbow.

"There's tea," he said. "The kettle's still hot."

I drank it and watched him work. Eventually I said, "Do you ever feel like you're only real when someone's watching you?"

He pressed the dough down with the heel of his hand. "I think," he said, "that's why I bake at night."

I thought he was being cryptic, the way Martin was. He wasn't. He was telling me the truth, and it would take me months to hear it.

I waited four days to tell Lizzy about the kiss. When I went looking for her, she wasn't on the balcony, but her phone was, face up beside the ashtray. It lit up with a message from Martin: *Did she tell you yet? Don't be cruel to her. She's young.*

It was the kindest thing Martin ever wrote about me, and it was the thing that undid me. I didn't read further. I'd like to call that integrity, but it was cowardice.

What I learned, I learned in pieces, the way you learn a dark room by walking into the furniture. Lizzy and Martin had been sleeping together since November, since the week she stopped coming to the group. Every time I described the bus stop, she had known exactly where he went after leaving me. And when Carl came to her, holding his worry in both hands like something he was afraid of spilling, and asked whether I was unhappy, Lizzy told him about the kiss.

Carl came to my room on a Sunday and sat with his coat still on. "I'd rather hear it from you," he said. So I told him everything, including how I had made myself smaller around him so there would be room for someone else. When I finished he folded his hands, and I thought, absurdly, of the receipts.

"I think you wanted someone to see you," he said. "I'm sorry I didn't know how."

"You did," I said. "I just didn't like what you saw."

He wasn't cruel about leaving, which was harder to bear than cruelty, because it left me nothing to push against except myself.

Lizzy tried once to explain, standing in the kitchen doorway in her enormous coat. "You know what he's like. He makes you feel like you're the only person who's ever had a thought." I did know. She hadn't stolen anything from me; she had wanted what I wanted and been better at taking it.

"Did he ask you to say more?" I asked.

She laughed, almost sadly. "Every time."

She went back to Leeds in May, leaving a cake outside my door, shaped like nothing in particular, with a note: *Sorry it fell. It always does.* I ate it alone at the kitchen window and cried, though not for the reasons I would have predicted.

I saw Martin once more, bent over a book in the Carolina Rediviva reading room. He looked older, and smaller, simply a man lonely in an articulate way, who borrowed other people's attention until he felt full. He didn't look up. I didn't wait for him to.

That spring I spent many nights in the kitchen with Johan. He taught me to test dough: press it with a finger and watch how slowly it comes back. "If it springs back fast, it needs more time. If it doesn't come back at all, you've waited too long." I asked if that was a metaphor. He looked genuinely confused and said, "No, it's bread," and I laughed for what felt like the first time in months.

I began to understand him. He wasn't hiding. He had found a way of doing something wholly, without needing a witness. The bread was real whether or not anyone saw it rise. I had spent the year trying to become real by being looked at, and had never once looked at myself the way Weil meant: with patient attention, the way you'd look at someone you love.

I won't say Johan and I fell in love; it wasn't like that. One night in June, when the sky stayed the color of weak tea until three in the morning, we carried a hot loaf onto the balcony and tore it open with our hands. Neither of us spoke. I was aware of him, and aware of myself, and for once the two didn't seem to be competing.

In autumn I went back to the reading group, now led by a woman from the theology faculty. In the first session she asked what Weil meant by attention, and the room went silent, and I felt the old pressure rise.

I didn't speak. I listened to the others, one by one, as they tried to work it out. It was the most generous thing I had ever done, and nobody noticed, and that was fine. That was, I was beginning to think, the whole point.
